claim: Predicting individual-level ethnicity from voter registration records and Census surname data via Bayes' rule (BISG) achieves 6% false-positive rate for Black voters and 3% for Latino voters while maintaining true-positive rate above 80%, validated against 9 million real Florida voter records with self-reported ethnicity.
stance_target: accuracy of individual-level covariate-based prediction methods as an alternative to classical ecological inference
scope_conditions: 9 million Florida voter registration records with self-reported ethnicity ground truth
quoted_support: We find that it is possible to reduce the false positive rate among Black and Latino voters to 6% and 3%, respectively, while maintaining the true positive rate above 80%.

claim: Turnout-by-race estimates derived from individual-level ethnicity prediction (BISG) yield substantially less bias and lower root mean squared error than standard ecological-inference estimates when validated against real self-reported ethnicity ground truth.
stance_target: individual-level prediction methods outperform classical aggregate ecological inference on point-estimate accuracy
scope_conditions: Florida voter file, real (not simulated) self-reported ethnicity
quoted_support: We use our predictions to estimate turnout by race and find that our estimates yields substantially less amounts of bias and root mean squared error than standard ecological inference estimates.

claim: All classical ecological-inference methods (Goodman 1953, King 1997, King/Rosen/Tanner 2004, Wakefield 2004) suffer from a fundamental indeterminacy problem, which has motivated the field's shift toward combining aggregate data with individual-level covariates rather than relying on aggregate-to-aggregate regression alone.
stance_target: classical ecological inference has known structural accuracy limitations independent of geographic scale
scope_conditions: general EI methodology, voting rights litigation and political behavior research context
quoted_support: Nevertheless, all of these methods suffer from a fundamental problem of indeterminacy, and as a result, in recent years, methodologists have turned to the idea of combining aggregate data with individual-level data.
